set.plain: LSD or mushrooms: what's actually different? One careful lab study gave 28 healthy adults both LSD and psilocybin, the drug in magic mushrooms, each on separate hospital days along with a dummy, in random order and without telling them which. The clearest difference was length: LSD's effects lasted about 9 to 11 hours on average, psilocybin's about 6 to 7. LSD also started a little sooner, which the authors put down to it being given as a liquid. Psilocybin's higher dose raised blood pressure and body temperature a little more, while LSD's higher dose raised heart rate more. Both brought complaints: on a checklist, 13 to 18 of the 28 had a headache in the first 12 hours after the drugs, against 8 on the dummy, and nobody had a serious problem. Otherwise, the trips were rated alike on almost every scale. But not finding a difference in 28 people does not prove there is none, and people named the right drug after 71 to 86 in 100 sessions, and the dummy after every session, which may have shaped their ratings. The study used pure psilocybin in capsules, not mushrooms, and did not test which amounts of the two drugs match.

set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: Registered, randomized, counterbalanced, double-dummy crossover with complete data for all 28 (N = 28 and F(4,108) in every supplementary table; card sc_holze_2022: RoB 2 some concerns). People named the right drug after 71 to 86 in 100 sessions and the dummy after every session (editors' calculation from Supplementary Table S8), so every subjective outcome, including the duration, which is modelled from self-ratings, was rated by people who often knew which drug they had; sequence generation and concealment are not described; the results text contradicts Supplementary Table S5 on heart rate after LSD 100 µg, two printed means lie outside their ranges, and 99 outcomes were each tested pairwise without correction across outcomes (editors' count of Table 1 and Supplementary Tables S1–S5). Blood pressure, heart rate and temperature are objective.
set.grade.domains.imprecision.note: 28 people. The duration difference is large and its test decisive, but 'no difference in kind' rests on non-significant post hoc tests without equivalence margins (Supplementary Tables S1–S4), and the differences in blood pressure, heart rate and temperature between the drugs are a few mmHg, a few beats a minute or a few tenths of a degree (Supplementary Table S5).

set.plain: What if you take LSD and MDMA at the same time? In one lab study, 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days: LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which. With both, blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone: top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone, and heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was no higher than on LSD alone. Bad feelings, fear and the number of complaints were not clearly lower than on LSD alone, and more people had trembling, restless legs or teeth grinding with both than with LSD alone. Nausea in the first 12 hours was reported by 11 of the 24 with both, 14 with MDMA alone, 7 with LSD alone and 4 with the dummy. The effects lasted about an hour and a half longer with both than with LSD alone (about 10 hours against 8.4 on average), and the longest lasted 21 hours. The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later. Nobody had a serious problem, but this was one amount of each drug, taken together by healthy people in a calm hospital room, so it says little about rare dangers or about a party.
